title: Secret Management
summary: Secrets — database passwords, API tokens, TLS certificates — must never be committed to Git or hardcoded in images. The DevOps ecosystem has several solutions: Kubernetes Secrets (baseline), External Secrets Operator (syncs from a secret store), HashiCorp Vault (full secret management), and Sealed Secrets (encrypted secrets in Git). The sandbox demonstrates External Secrets Operator.

sections.title: The secrets problem: why plaintext fails
sections.body:
## Why secrets need to be treated differently from all other configuration

A **secret** is any piece of data that grants access or proves identity — a database password, an API token, a TLS private key, an OAuth client secret. Unlike a port number or a feature flag, a leaked secret can cause immediate, irreversible harm: an attacker who finds your database password in a GitHub commit can exfiltrate every row before you have time to rotate it.

The core danger is **persistence**. Git is designed to remember everything. Even if you delete a file containing a password and push a new commit, the secret lives in the repository's full history, in every clone, in every fork, in the reflog. Automated scanners — including those run by attackers — continuously crawl GitHub for credential patterns. The average time between a secret being committed and a bot harvesting it is measured in **seconds**.

Beyond Git, secrets find their way into Docker image layers (visible via `docker history`), CI/CD logs, Kubernetes manifest files, and environment variable dumps. Each location is a separate blast radius: a developer's laptop, a container registry, a CD pipeline, a monitoring dashboard.

**The fundamental principle** is that secrets must be separated from code and configuration, stored in a dedicated secret store, and injected into workloads at runtime — never baked in at build time. Secret stores provide three things code repositories cannot: **encryption at rest and in transit**, **access control** (audit who read what and when), and **rotation** (change the secret without redeploying every service).

Understanding why each anti-pattern fails — and what "base64 encoding" actually means — is the foundation for choosing the right tool for each use case.

**The anti-patterns:**

```bash norun
# ✗ Hardcoded in source code
DB_PASSWORD = "<CHANGE_ME>"     # visible to anyone with repo access

# ✗ In .env files committed to Git
echo 'DB_PASSWORD=<CHANGE_ME>' >> .env
git add .env && git commit -m "add config"  # now it's in git history forever

# ✗ In Docker images (docker history exposes them)
FROM python:3.12
ENV DB_PASSWORD=<CHANGE_ME>     # visible in image layers

# ✗ In Kubernetes manifests checked into Git
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  password: c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=  # base64 is NOT encryption!
```

**What base64 is not:**

```bash
# base64 is encoding, not encryption
echo '<CHANGE_ME>' | base64
# c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=

# Trivially reversed:
echo 'c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=' | base64 -d
# <CHANGE_ME>

# Kubernetes Secrets are base64 in etcd by default
# Anyone with kubectl access to the Secret can decode it
# Enable etcd encryption at rest for real protection
```

**Secret rotation problem:**

```
When credentials are hardcoded, rotation means:
1. Update every place the secret is hardcoded
2. Redeploy all services that use it
3. Hope you didn't miss any

With a secret manager:
1. Rotate in the secret manager
2. Applications automatically pick up the new value
   (via environment injection or secret reload)
```

**The CIA triad applied to secrets:**

```
Confidentiality — only authorized services/users can read the secret
               (RBAC, access policies, audit logs)

Integrity      — secrets cannot be tampered with undetected
               (audit trail, versioning, signing)

Availability   — services can always fetch their secrets
               (HA secret store, caching, fallback mechanisms)
```

sections.title: Kubernetes Secrets: the baseline
sections.body:
## Kubernetes Secrets: the cluster-native secret primitive

Kubernetes Secrets are the built-in mechanism for storing sensitive data inside a cluster. They exist as first-class API objects, meaning they participate in the same RBAC, namespacing, and watch/notify systems as any other Kubernetes resource. Many cluster components — the kubelet pulling private images, the ingress controller serving TLS, the service mesh doing mTLS — depend on Secrets internally.

**How Secrets work at the storage layer:** When you create a Secret, Kubernetes stores it in **etcd**, the distributed key-value database that backs the entire cluster state. By default, the data is stored as-is (base64-encoded for historical reasons, but not encrypted). Etcd encryption at rest is an opt-in feature that must be explicitly configured on the API server with an `EncryptionConfiguration` object. Without it, anyone who can read the etcd data volume — or run `kubectl get secret -o yaml` — can recover the plaintext.

**The three consumption patterns** for Secrets — environment variables, `envFrom` bulk injection, and volume mounts — have different security trade-offs. Environment variables are convenient but are visible in process listings, crash dumps, and any code that calls `os.environ`. Volume mounts (files at a path) are more controlled: the file can have restrictive permissions, can be updated without restarting the pod (when using a mounted volume rather than env vars), and can be monitored for access.

**RBAC is the primary access control layer for Secrets.** Because `kubectl get secrets` in a namespace returns every secret, least-privilege design requires scoping access to specific secret names using `resourceNames`. A pod's ServiceAccount should be able to read exactly the secrets it needs — nothing more.

Understanding these trade-offs explains why native Kubernetes Secrets are the *target format* for all secret management tools, even when the source of truth is Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.

```bash
# Create secrets imperatively
kubectl create secret generic db-credentials \
  --from-literal=username=appuser \
  --from-literal=password=<CHANGE_ME>

# kubectl create secret generic tls-certs \
#   --from-file=tls.crt=./server.crt \
#   --from-file=tls.key=./server.key   # (requires actual cert files)

# Create a Docker registry secret (image pull)
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io \
  --docker-username=myuser \
  --docker-password=<YOUR_REGISTRY_TOKEN>

# View secrets (base64 encoded)
kubectl get secret db-credentials -o yaml

# Decode a specific field
kubectl get secret db-credentials \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
```

**Consuming secrets in pods:**

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:v1

    # Method 1: environment variables from secret
    env:
    - name: DB_PASSWORD
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-credentials
          key: password

    # Method 2: inject all keys as env vars
    envFrom:
    - secretRef:
        name: db-credentials

    # Method 3: mount as files
    volumeMounts:
    - name: certs
      mountPath: /etc/certs
      readOnly: true

  volumes:
  - name: certs
    secret:
      secretName: tls-certs
```

**RBAC for secrets:**

```yaml
# Restrict secret access — only the app SA can read its secret
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: secret-reader
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]
  resourceNames: ["db-credentials"]  # only THIS secret
  verbs: ["get"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: app-reads-secret
  namespace: production
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: my-app
  namespace: production
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: secret-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

**Limitations of native Kubernetes Secrets:**

```
✗ Not encrypted in etcd by default
✗ Still stored in Kubernetes (what if cluster is compromised?)
✗ No rotation — secrets don't auto-update in running pods
✗ No audit trail of who read what
✗ YAML manifests can't be stored in Git without being a secret
```

sections.title: External Secrets Operator: syncing from a secret store
sections.body:
## External Secrets Operator: bridging your secret store and Kubernetes

Organizations running production workloads rarely use Kubernetes Secrets as their *source of truth* — they use a dedicated secret management system such as AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault. These systems provide encryption, access auditing, versioning, and rotation workflows that etcd-backed Secrets cannot match.

The **External Secrets Operator (ESO)** is a CNCF project that acts as a bridge. It runs as a controller inside the cluster, watches custom resources you define (`ExternalSecret` objects), fetches the corresponding secrets from the external store, and creates or updates native Kubernetes `Secret` objects automatically. Your application code continues to read Kubernetes Secrets via the standard API — it never needs to know that the backing store is Vault or Secrets Manager.

This architecture has several important properties. First, **zero-secret-in-Git**: you commit an `ExternalSecret` manifest (which only names the path in the external store, not the value), and ESO fetches the actual value at runtime. Second, **automatic rotation**: ESO polls the external store on a configurable interval (`refreshInterval`). When a secret is rotated in the external store, ESO creates an updated Kubernetes Secret within that interval — no manual intervention, no pod restart required if you use volume mounts or a reloader. Third, **centralised access control**: the IAM or Vault policy that grants ESO access to the secret store is the single chokepoint for all cluster-to-secret-store communication.

The two core ESO objects are `SecretStore` (or `ClusterSecretStore` for cluster-wide scope), which defines *how to authenticate* to the external store, and `ExternalSecret`, which defines *what to fetch* and *where to put it* in Kubernetes.

```
External Secret Store          ESO Operator          Kubernetes
(AWS Secrets Manager,    →    (controller)      →   Secret object
 GCP Secret Manager,          polls & syncs
 Vault, etc.)
```

**Key ESO objects:**

```yaml
# SecretStore — defines HOW to connect to the secret store
# (namespace-scoped; use ClusterSecretStore for cluster-wide)
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secretsmanager
  namespace: production
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        secretRef:
          accessKeyIDSecretRef:
            name: aws-creds
            key: access-key-id
          secretAccessKeySecretRef:
            name: aws-creds
            key: secret-access-key
```

```yaml
# ExternalSecret — defines WHAT to sync
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  namespace: production
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h          # re-sync every hour
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secretsmanager
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: db-credentials       # name of Kubernetes Secret to create
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: username      # key in Kubernetes Secret
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/db           # path in Secrets Manager
        property: username     # JSON field within the secret
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/db
        property: password
```

**Check ESO in the sandbox:**

```bash
# ESO is installed in the sandbox
kubectl get pods -n external-secrets
# Shows: external-secrets controller, cert-controller, webhook

# Check CRDs
kubectl get crds | grep external-secrets
# externalsecrets.external-secrets.io
# secretstores.external-secrets.io
# clustersecretstores.external-secrets.io

# View any configured ClusterSecretStores
kubectl get clustersecretstores

# View ExternalSecrets across all namespaces
kubectl get externalsecrets -A

# Check ESO sync status
kubectl describe externalsecret db-credentials -n production
# Status.Conditions shows if sync succeeded
```

**ESO with Vault:**

```yaml
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: vault-backend
spec:
  provider:
    vault:
      server: https://vault.example.com:8200
      path: secret
      version: v2
      auth:
        kubernetes:
          mountPath: kubernetes
          role: my-app-role
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: external-secrets
            namespace: external-secrets
```

sections.title: HashiCorp Vault: full secret lifecycle management
sections.body:
## HashiCorp Vault: the industry standard for secret lifecycle management

HashiCorp Vault is a purpose-built secret management system that goes well beyond storing key-value pairs. Its core insight is that **secrets should be ephemeral**: rather than storing long-lived credentials that must be manually rotated, Vault can *generate* credentials on demand and automatically revoke them when they expire. This transforms the rotation problem from an operational burden into an automated process.

**The secret engine model** is Vault's most important architectural concept. A secret engine is a plugin that handles a category of secrets. The `kv-v2` engine stores static key-value pairs with versioning. The `database` engine connects to a real database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB) and generates unique username/password pairs for each requester, valid for a configurable TTL. The `pki` engine is a full certificate authority that issues short-lived TLS certificates. The `aws` engine generates temporary IAM access keys. This means a service can receive a database credential that exists for exactly one hour and is then revoked in the database automatically — no rotation script needed.

**Authentication methods** determine how a client proves its identity to Vault before receiving a secret. The Kubernetes auth method is the standard for in-cluster workloads: a pod presents its ServiceAccount JWT token, Vault validates it against the Kubernetes API, and if the token's ServiceAccount matches a configured role, Vault issues a Vault token with the appropriate policies attached.

**Leases and renewal** give every Vault secret a time-to-live. The Vault Agent sidecar handles token renewal and secret caching transparently, ensuring the application always has a valid credential without being aware of Vault's internal lifecycle.

**Sealed Secrets** (from Bitnami) takes a different approach: it lets you encrypt secrets using a controller's public key so that the encrypted form is safe to commit to Git, where it is decrypted by the controller at apply time. This suits GitOps workflows where the entire cluster state must live in a repository.

**Vault concepts:**

```
Secret Engine   — backend that stores or generates secrets
                (kv-v2: key-value store, database: dynamic DB creds,
                 pki: certificate authority, aws: dynamic IAM creds)

Authentication  — how a client proves its identity
                (kubernetes: pod uses SA token, aws: IAM role,
                 ldap: corporate directory, approle: machine auth)

Policy          — what paths a token can access
                (path "secret/data/myapp/*" { capabilities = ["read"] })

Lease           — TTL on a secret (dynamic creds expire automatically)

Audit Device    — logs every request (file, syslog, socket)
```

**Core Vault operations:**

```bash norun
# Set Vault address and token
export VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com:8200
export VAULT_TOKEN=s.xyzABCdef123

# Write a secret
vault kv put secret/myapp/db \
  username=appuser \
  password=<CHANGE_ME>

# Read a secret
vault kv get secret/myapp/db
vault kv get -field=password secret/myapp/db

# List secrets at a path
vault kv list secret/myapp/

# Check your token's permissions
vault token lookup
vault token capabilities secret/myapp/db

# Dynamic database credentials (Vault generates them on-demand)
vault read database/creds/my-role
# Output: username=v-app-aB3xYz, password=A1b2C3d4..., lease_duration=1h
# → When TTL expires, credentials are revoked in the database automatically
```

**Vault Agent: auto-inject secrets into pods:**

```yaml
# Vault Agent Injector annotation-based injection
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-app
  annotations:
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
    vault.hashicorp.com/role: "my-app-role"
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db.env: "secret/data/myapp/db"
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-db.env: |
      {{- with secret "secret/data/myapp/db" -}}
      export DB_USERNAME={{ .Data.data.username }}
      export DB_PASSWORD={{ .Data.data.password }}
      {{- end }}
spec:
  serviceAccountName: my-app  # used for Vault k8s auth
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp:v1
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "source /vault/secrets/db.env && ./start.sh"]
```

**Sealed Secrets: encrypted secrets in Git:**

```bash norun
# Sealed Secrets controller runs in K8s, holds the private key
# kubeseal CLI encrypts secrets using the controller's public key

# Install kubeseal
curl -sSL https://github.com/bitnami-labs/sealed-secrets/releases/download/v0.24.5/kubeseal-0.24.5-linux-amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
mv kubeseal /usr/local/bin/

# Create a sealed secret from a regular secret
kubectl create secret generic db-password \
  --from-literal=password=<CHANGE_ME> \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | \
  kubeseal --format=yaml > sealed-db-password.yaml

# The output is safe to commit to Git — only the controller can decrypt it
cat sealed-db-password.yaml
git add sealed-db-password.yaml && git commit -m "add sealed db password"

# ArgoCD syncs it → controller decrypts it → creates a real Secret
kubectl get secret db-password  # now exists as a regular Secret
```

sections.title: Exercise: explore ESO and secret patterns in the sandbox
sections.body:
## Putting it together: hands-on exploration

Secret management concepts become concrete when you interact with the running system. This exercise walks through the External Secrets Operator installation, the lifecycle of a Kubernetes Secret, environment variable injection into a pod, and the rotation problem — specifically why pods do not automatically pick up updated secrets when secrets are injected as environment variables.

Pay attention to the difference between what the operator reports in its status conditions versus what the actual Kubernetes Secret contains. Understanding the sync loop — ESO fetches from external store, writes to Kubernetes, Kubernetes mounts into pod — tells you exactly where to look when things go wrong in production.

The rotation simulation at the end demonstrates a critical operational point: **environment variable injection is a snapshot taken at pod start time**. If you update a Secret after a pod is running, the environment variable inside the pod does not change. This is why production systems use either mounted volume secrets (Kubernetes updates these in-place, though the application must re-read the file) or a controller like Reloader that automatically restarts deployments when their referenced Secrets change.

```bash
# ── 1. Inspect the ESO installation ──────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get pods -n external-secrets
kubectl get crds | grep external-secrets

# ── 2. Check what secret stores are configured ────────────────────────────
kubectl get clustersecretstores
kubectl get secretstores -A

# ── 3. Look at existing ExternalSecrets ───────────────────────────────────
kubectl get externalsecrets -A
if kubectl get externalsecret db-credentials -n learning 2>/dev/null; then
  kubectl describe externalsecret db-credentials -n learning
fi

# ── 4. Explore Kubernetes Secrets in the sandbox ──────────────────────────
# List all secrets (don't print values in a real system!)
kubectl get secrets -A | grep -v 'kubernetes.io/service-account'

# Look at the ArgoCD admin secret:
kubectl get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -n argocd -o yaml

# Decode it:
kubectl get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -n argocd \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d && echo

# ── 5. Create a secret and consume it ────────────────────────────────────
kubectl create secret generic test-secret -n learning \
  --from-literal=api-key=my-super-secret-api-key \
  --from-literal=db-url=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb

# Verify it exists:
kubectl get secret test-secret -n learning -o yaml

# ── 6. Deploy a pod that reads the secret as env vars ─────────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-consumer
  namespace: learning
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo API_KEY=$API_KEY && echo DB_URL=$DB_URL && sleep 60"]
    env:
    - name: API_KEY
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: test-secret
          key: api-key
    - name: DB_URL
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: test-secret
          key: db-url
  restartPolicy: Never
EOF

# Wait for it to start:
kubectl wait pod/secret-consumer -n learning --for=condition=ready --timeout=30s

# See the injected secrets:
kubectl logs secret-consumer -n learning

# ── 7. Secret rotation simulation ─────────────────────────────────────────
# Update the secret:
kubectl create secret generic test-secret -n learning \
  --from-literal=api-key=rotated-new-api-key \
  --from-literal=db-url=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Note: running pods do NOT automatically get the new value
# (env var injection is at pod start time)
# To pick up the new secret, the pod must be restarted
# (This is why mounted volume secrets or ESO with reloader is better)

# ── 8. Clean up ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete pod secret-consumer -n learning
kubectl delete secret test-secret -n learning
```
